title: Gauss-Wilson Theorem: Product of Units and Cyclic Groups
description: Formalizes the Gauss-Wilson theorem: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, proved via involution lemma and self-inverse classification. Full proof that cyclic → product = -1 and non-cyclic → product = 1. Verifies Gauss-Wilson for all n ≤ 300 and confirms no Wilson primes between 14 and 100. 21 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Gauss-Wilson theorem originated in Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801): the product of all units mod n equals -1 exactly when (ℤ/nℤ)* has a primitive root — equivalently when (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic — which occurs iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} for odd prime p. The proof strategy — pairing group elements with their inverses — is a classical argument: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel, leaving only the self-inverse elements (those with x² = 1). For cyclic groups this set is {1, -1}, giving product = -1. For non-cyclic groups the self-inverse elements form an elementary abelian 2-group of size ≥ 4, forcing the product to 1. Formalizing this in Lean requires Finset.prod_involution (the pairing lemma), IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le (the cyclic group cardinality bound), and the concrete-abstract bridge via Finset.prod_nbij. The non-cyclic case is handled in a companion file WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext using a fixed-point-free involution with constant pair product.
overview.problemStatement: For which n is ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 (mod n)? Prove it equals -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, using the involution pairing lemma.
overview.text: The key proof is the involution lemma: in any finite abelian group G, pair each element with its inverse. Elements not equal to their inverse cancel in pairs. The remaining product is ∏{x | x²=1}. In a cyclic group with n≥3, the only self-inverse elements are 1 and -1, so ∏{x | x²=1} = -1. In a non-cyclic unit group, there exists a Klein-four subgroup, and the product of a Klein-four group is 1, making the total product 1. This gives the complete characterization.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove the involution lemma: ∏G = ∏{x : x²=1} via Finset.prod_involution. Prove cyclic unit groups have exactly {1,-1} as self-inverse elements using IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le + sandwich. Prove non-cyclic case via WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext. Combine for the biconditional. Bridge to concrete unitsProduct via Finset.prod_nbij.
keyInsights: Involution product lemma: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel via Finset.prod_involution; ∏G reduces to ∏{x | x²=1}
Cyclic sandwich: |{x|x²=1}| ≤ 2 (IsCyclic) and {1,-1} ⊆ {x|x²=1} with -1≠1, so {x|x²=1} = {1,-1} exactly
Non-cyclic: the self-inverse set forms an elementary abelian 2-group of size ≥ 4, handled by WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext via fixed-point-free involution
Concrete-abstract bridge: unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract via Finset.prod_nbij with bijection x ↦ ZMod.val(x)
The proof is purely group-theoretic: independent of the specific ring structure of ℤ/nℤ
Computational confidence: gaussWilson_verified_le_300 and no Wilson primes in [14,100] verified by native_decide
prerequisites: Finite abelian groups: Finset.prod_involution, pairing with inverses
Klein-four group: elementary abelian 2-groups and their products

conclusion.summary: Gauss-Wilson theorem proved abstract and concrete: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 ↔ IsCyclic (ZMod n)ˣ, via involution product lemma, self-inverse classification in cyclic groups, Klein-four argument for non-cyclic case, and Finset.prod_nbij bridge. Computationally verified for n ≤ 300; no Wilson primes in [14, 100]. 21 theorems, 8 definitions, 426 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The Gauss-Wilson theorem is the algebraic foundation for primitive root theory: (ℤ/nℤ)* cyclic iff primitive roots exist mod n, characterizing the n where the discrete logarithm is well-defined. The involution product lemma is a general technique applicable to any finite abelian group product computation. The companion WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext provides the non-cyclic case via a fixed-point-free involution with constant pair product — a technique applicable beyond this setting.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many Wilson primes? Equivalent to: are there infinitely many p with p | B_{p-1}?
Formalize the non-cyclic case without the companion file: direct involution argument in WilsonsTheoremOQ02
Generalize to Dedekind domains: product of units in OK where K is a number field
Formalize the connection: Wilson prime ↔ irregular prime of a particular type (p | numerator of B_{p-1})

sections.title: Abstract Units Product and Prime Case
sections.description: abstractUnitsProduct definition. prod_units_eq_neg_one_prime: Wilson's theorem via Mathlib's FiniteField.prod_univ_units_id_eq_neg_one. units_val_prod helper for coercing products.
sections.summary: Defines abstractUnitsProduct n = ∏ x : (ZMod n)ˣ, (x : ZMod n) and proves Wilson's theorem (prime case) by invoking Mathlib's FiniteField.prod_univ_units_id_eq_neg_one. units_val_prod bridges the abstract units product to ZMod arithmetic.
sections.mathContext: $\text{abstractUnitsProduct}(n) := \prod_{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times} x \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. For prime $p$: $\prod_{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times} x = -1$ via $\texttt{FiniteField.prod\_univ\_units\_id\_eq\_neg\_one}$, reducing Wilson's theorem to a single Mathlib finite-field lemma without manual inverse-pairing.

sections.title: Self-Inverse Elements and Their Structure
sections.description: sq_eq_one_iff_eq_inv (x²=1 iff x=x⁻¹), selfInverseUnits definition (Finset.univ.filter for x²=1 elements).
sections.summary: Proves sq_eq_one_iff_eq_inv: in any commutative group, x² = 1 iff x = x⁻¹. Defines selfInverseUnits n = Finset.univ.filter (fun x => x ^ 2 = 1) as the subfinset of order-≤2 units.
sections.mathContext: $x^2 = 1 \iff x = x^{-1}$ in any commutative group (since $x \cdot x = 1 \iff x = x^{-1}$). $\text{selfInverseUnits}(n) = \{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times : x^2 = 1\}$. These are the fixed points of the involution $a \mapsto a^{-1}$; all other elements pair up as $(a, a^{-1})$ with $a \neq a^{-1}$, contributing product 1.

sections.title: Distinctness of -1 and 1 for n≥3
sections.description: neg_one_ne_one_units and neg_one_ne_one_zmod for n≥3. Proved by showing n | -2 forces n ≤ 2 via Int.le_of_dvd.
sections.summary: Proves neg_one_ne_one_units and neg_one_ne_one_zmod: for n ≥ 3, -1 ≠ 1 in (ZMod n)ˣ and ZMod n respectively. The key: if -1 = 1 then n | 2, which forces n ≤ 2 via Int.le_of_dvd, contradicting n ≥ 3.
sections.mathContext: In $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$: $-1 = 1 \iff n \mid 2 \iff n \in \{1, 2\}$. For $n \geq 3$: $-1 \neq 1$, so $|\{1,-1\}| = 2$. Proof: $-1 = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ means $n \mid (-1-1) = -2$, hence $n \leq 2$ by $\texttt{Int.le\_of\_dvd}$, contradicting $n \geq 3$.

sections.title: Cyclic Group Infrastructure
sections.description: isCyclic_units_prime (IsCyclic for prime ZMod), card_sq_eq_one_le_two (|{x|x²=1}| ≤ 2 for cyclic groups), selfInverse_units_eq_pair ({x|x²=1} = {1,-1} for cyclic n≥3).
sections.summary: Proves three lemmas: isCyclic_units_prime (prime → (ZMod p)ˣ is cyclic), card_sq_eq_one_le_two (cyclic → at most 2 solutions to x²=1), and selfInverse_units_eq_pair (cyclic + n≥3 → {x|x²=1} = {1,-1} via sandwich argument).
sections.mathContext: For cyclic $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$: the number of solutions to $x^k = 1$ divides $k$ (since subgroups of cyclic groups are unique of each order), so $|\{x : x^2=1\}| \leq 2$. Combined with $\{1,-1\} \subseteq \{x:x^2=1\}$ and $|-1 \neq 1|$ for $n \geq 3$: sandwich gives $\{x:x^2=1\} = \{1,-1\}$ exactly. Via $\texttt{IsCyclic.card\_pow\_eq\_one\_le}$.

sections.title: Klein-Four Building Block
sections.description: mul_sq_eq_one_of_sq_eq_one (closure under order-2 multiplication), prod_klein_four (product of {1,a,b,ab} = 1 when a²=b²=1). Key lemma for the non-cyclic case.
sections.summary: Proves mul_sq_eq_one_of_sq_eq_one (the self-inverse elements form a subgroup: if a²=b²=1 then (ab)²=1) and prod_klein_four: for the Klein-four subgroup {1,a,b,ab} with a²=b²=1 and a,b,ab pairwise distinct, the product equals 1.
sections.mathContext: The Klein-four group $V_4 = \{1, a, b, ab\}$ satisfies $a^2 = b^2 = (ab)^2 = 1$ and all elements are self-inverse. Its product: $1 \cdot a \cdot b \cdot ab = (a \cdot a)(b \cdot b) = 1$. For non-cyclic $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$: since $|\{x:x^2=1\}| \geq 4$ (non-cyclic has more than 2 square roots of unity), the product over $\{x:x^2=1\}$ equals $1$, giving $\prod G = 1$.

sections.title: Involution Product Lemma
sections.description: prod_univ_sq_eq_one ((∏G)² = 1 via bijection g↦g⁻¹), prod_eq_prod_sq_eq_one (∏G = ∏{x|x²=1} via Finset.prod_involution). The structural heart of the theorem.
sections.summary: Proves prod_univ_sq_eq_one ((∏G)² = 1 via the bijection g ↦ g⁻¹ pairing all elements) and prod_eq_prod_sq_eq_one (∏G = ∏{x|x²=1}): non-self-inverse elements cancel in inverse pairs via Finset.prod_involution. This is the structural core enabling both the cyclic and non-cyclic product computations.
sections.mathContext: For any finite commutative group $G$: $\prod_{g \in G} g = \prod_{\substack{x \in G \\ x^2=1}} x$. Proof: apply $\texttt{Finset.prod\_involution}$ with the involution $\sigma(a) = a^{-1}$. Fixed points: $\{a : a = a^{-1}\} = \{a : a^2 = 1\}$. Non-fixed pairs $(a, a^{-1})$ contribute $a \cdot a^{-1} = 1$. So only self-inverse elements contribute to the product. Separately, $(\prod_G g)^2 = \prod_G g \cdot \prod_G g^{-1} = 1$ since $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ is a bijection.

sections.title: Cyclic and Non-Cyclic Product Formulas
sections.description: prod_units_neg_one_of_cyclic (cyclic n≥3 → ∏ = -1 via involution + {1,-1}), prod_units_one_of_not_cyclic (non-cyclic → ∏ = 1 via WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext).
sections.summary: Assembles the two directions: prod_units_neg_one_of_cyclic chains involution lemma → selfInverse_units_eq_pair → ∏{1,-1} = -1. prod_units_one_of_not_cyclic delegates to WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext (fixed-point-free involution argument for non-cyclic case).
sections.mathContext: Cyclic, $n \geq 3$: $\prod_{(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times} x \xrightarrow{\text{invol.}} \prod_{x^2=1} x = \prod_{\{1,-1\}} x = 1 \cdot (-1) = -1$. Non-cyclic: $|\{x:x^2=1\}| \geq 4$ (non-cyclic has $\geq 4$ square roots of unity), the product over $\{x:x^2=1\}$ splits into pairs each with product $1$ (via fixed-point-free involution in OQ02Ext), giving $\prod = 1$. Together these give the complete biconditional.

sections.title: Gauss-Wilson Abstract Biconditional
sections.description: gaussWilson_abstract: for n≥3, ∏(ZMod n)ˣ = -1 iff IsCyclic (ZMod n)ˣ. The main theorem combining both directions.
sections.summary: Proves gaussWilson_abstract: for n ≥ 3, the abstract units product ∏(ZMod n)ˣ = -1 iff (ZMod n)ˣ is cyclic. Forward direction by contradiction (non-cyclic gives product = 1 ≠ -1); backward direction by prod_units_neg_one_of_cyclic.
sections.mathContext: $\forall n \geq 3: \prod_{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times} x = -1 \iff (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \text{ is cyclic}$. $(\Leftarrow)$: cyclic $\Rightarrow$ product $= -1$ by $\texttt{prod\_units\_neg\_one\_of\_cyclic}$. $(\Rightarrow)$: if $\neg$cyclic, product $= 1$ by $\texttt{prod\_units\_one\_of\_not\_cyclic}$; since $-1 \neq 1$ for $n \geq 3$, product $= -1$ implies cyclic by contrapositive.

sections.title: Concrete-Abstract Bridge
sections.description: unitsProduct concrete definition, unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract: (unitsProduct n : ZMod n) = ∏(ZMod n)ˣ via Finset.prod_nbij with bijection x ↦ ZMod.val(x).
sections.summary: Defines unitsProduct n as the concrete Finset product over {a < n | Nat.Coprime a n} and proves unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract: casting to ZMod n equals the abstract group product ∏(ZMod n)ˣ. Uses Finset.prod_nbij with bijection x ↦ ZMod.val(x).
sections.mathContext: $\text{unitsProduct}(n) := \prod_{\substack{a < n \\ \gcd(a,n)=1}} a \in \mathbb{N}$. Bridge: $(\text{unitsProduct}(n) : \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) = \prod_{x \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times} x$ (abstract units product). Bijection: $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \xrightarrow{\text{val}} \{a < n : \gcd(a,n)=1\}$ via $\texttt{ZMod.val}$, $\texttt{ZMod.unitOfCoprime}$; reindexed via $\texttt{Finset.prod\_nbij}$. Imported by OQ01 to connect concrete modular arithmetic to gaussWilson_abstract.

sections.title: Computational Verification to n≤300
sections.description: hasGaussWilsonForm, gaussWilsonCheck definitions. gaussWilson_verified_le_250 and gaussWilson_verified_le_300 via native_decide.
sections.summary: Defines hasGaussWilsonForm n (decidable check: n = 1, 2, 4, or n = p^k or 2p^k for odd prime p) and gaussWilsonCheck n (unitsProduct ≡ -1 iff hasGaussWilsonForm). Proves gaussWilson_verified_le_250 and gaussWilson_verified_le_300 by native_decide exhaustive computation.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{hasGaussWilsonForm}(n)$: decidable predicate for $n \in \{1,2,4,p^k,2p^k\}$ (odd prime $p$). $\texttt{gaussWilsonCheck}(n)$: verifies $\prod_{\gcd(a,n)=1} a \equiv -1 \pmod{n} \iff \texttt{hasGaussWilsonForm}(n)$. $\texttt{native\_decide}$ compiles to native code for fast exhaustive verification: confirms the theorem for all $n \leq 300$ without a single algebraic argument — a computational certificate complementing the abstract proof.

sections.title: Wilson Primes: Definitions and Verification
sections.description: wilsonQuotient, IsWilsonPrime definitions. five_is_wilson_prime, thirteen_is_wilson_prime verified. no_wilson_primes_14_to_100 via native_decide over Fin 101.
sections.summary: Defines wilsonQuotient p = ((p-1)! + 1) / p and IsWilsonPrime p (p² | (p-1)! + 1). Verifies five_is_wilson_prime and thirteen_is_wilson_prime by norm_num. Proves no_wilson_primes_14_to_100 via native_decide over Fin 101: no Wilson prime exists in [14, 100].
sections.mathContext: $W_p := \frac{(p-1)!+1}{p}$ (Wilson quotient, always a positive integer by Wilson's theorem for primes). $p$ is a Wilson prime iff $p \mid W_p$ iff $p^2 \mid (p-1)!+1$. Verified: $W_5 = 5$, $W_{13} = 13$ (Wilson primes). $\texttt{native\_decide}$: for all primes $p \in [14,100]$, $p^2 \nmid (p-1)!+1$. Known Wilson primes: $\{5, 13, 563\}$ — no fourth is known; search extended to $\approx 2 \times 10^{13}$.
